source.title: Revisiting Neural Scaling Laws in Language and Vision
source.authors: Ibrahim M. Alabdulmohsin; Behnam Neyshabur; Xiao-Hua Zhai

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates scaling-law fits and extrapolation with its own experiments, using a different estimator-comparison methodology from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports extrapolation results for language modeling, image classification, NMT and BIG-Bench tasks. The NMT results are not included as rows because they measure translation log-perplexity rather than the language-model pretraining or downstream measures named by the claim versions. Image and BIG-Bench results are recorded as the paper's stated aggregates where it does not provide a single aggregate numeric value. Values cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Fits power-law estimators to LM, NMT, vision and BIG-Bench learning curves and scores held-out extrapolation. It argues that best-fitting (interpolating) exponents can mislead, which bears on V7, and reports short-horizon extrapolation quality, which bears on V2. The main comparison is the authors' estimator M4 against prior forms, so many rows are method comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that best-fitting scaling parameters need not extrapolate best, so laws should be validated by extrapolation loss. They propose M4, which extrapolates better across image, NMT, LM and BIG-Bench tasks. They note M2 performs similarly to M4 in LM, with LM exponents near -1/3 shrinking with model size, while vision exponents grow with model size.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares four learning-curve estimator families using a held-out portion of each curve and proposes M4; it does not reproduce the original parameter/data/compute scaling or compute-optimal-allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Extrapolation quality and selected exponent depend on estimator form and on whether parameters are chosen by interpolation or extrapolation. The paper also reports different exponent trends by model size and domain.
record.problems: The language-model prediction test evaluates the second half of learning curves rather than runs orders of magnitude larger. Validation loss is rescaled to [0, 1]. Several image and BIG-Bench findings are reported as aggregates; some underlying datasets are proprietary. The paper's stated limits include noisy BIG-Bench learning curves.
record.rows_left_out: NMT rows are omitted because the reported outcome is translation log-perplexity, not the language-model pretraining or downstream measures named by the claim versions. The task-specific BIG-Bench Table 3 values are not separately transcribed because the paper's aggregate conclusion is recorded in BIGBENCH-AGG. The image-domain task-level estimator results are summarized by the reported aggregate in IMAGE-AGG.

untested.parts: Parameter-count and compute scaling; ranges beyond about two decades of tokens; separate data-limited runs.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger; the horizon is only 2x tokens within the same run.
Video, fine-tuning; the vision power-law and repeated-data evidence is not captured in rows.
Prediction from pretraining loss; scale in parameters; tasks beyond five selected for high learnability.
Parameter counting, training schedule and data choices; compute-optimal split.

missing.what: ViT/B/16 ImageNet 10-shot error vs JFT examples follows a linear log-log curve (power law emerges) in a vision transfer setting
Vision scaling exponents by architecture: larger models in each family have more favourable (larger |c|) exponents, opposite to the LM trend; M4 gives larger |c| than M2
Repeated (bootstrapped) JFT examples behave like fresh samples until overfitting peaks; 12M subset overfits
NMT held-out log-perplexity extrapolation from 256M to 512M sentence pairs for five architectures, by estimator
Per-task, per-shot BIG-Bench extrapolation RMSEs (e.g. M2 date_understanding 3.2e-2 vs M3 4.7e-3)
Synthetic logistic regression: M2 exponent estimates vary from -0.14 to -0.48 with cutoff when data are outside the power-law regime

record.verdict_notes: Table 2 text is garbled. The record's assignment of LM values (M3 beating M2 everywhere) conflicts with the text's statement that M2 and M4 are best for LM; check the PDF before using the numbers. RMSE is on log values of loss rescaled to [0,1], i.e. relative error. All extrapolations are 2x along a single training curve. M4 rows are the authors' own method and were not used as V2 evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Tests language-model validation loss against token count, but does not test parameter-count or compute scaling; the tested range does not establish a power law over several orders of magnitude.
Tests extrapolation from the first part of learning curves to the second part, not prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget search or comparison of parameter/token allocations.
Does not compare depth, width or other architecture details at fixed parameter count for loss.
Tests image-classification transfer curves, but not video, repeated-data training, fine-tuning or transfer regimes beyond the described few-shot transfer evaluation.
Tests a limited set of five selected BIG-Bench tasks and few-shot image-classification metrics; does not establish downstream predictability generally.
Does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedules or data choices for the compute-optimal allocation; that allocation is not tested.

rows.subject: LaMDA
rows.size_stated: Five model sizes ranging from 107 to 109 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit scaling estimators to validation-loss learning curves over token count and report estimated exponents across model sizes.
rows.measure: Estimated scaling exponent c as model size varies
rows.value: For M2 and M4, c is close to −1/3 and decreases in absolute magnitude for larger models; M1 and M3 give small absolute estimates.
rows.note: The paper describes the trends and plots the exponents; it does not state the individual plotted exponent values in text.
rows.check: For V1, excess loss follows a power law in tokens (~1e9 to 1e11) only once an asymptote is included (M2/M4, c≈-1/3); M1 gives tiny exponents. The curves are within-run training curves, not separate data-limited runs. For V7, the exponent depends on estimator and shrinks with model size.

rows.subject: ViT/B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compare the M2 exponent giving the best fit to the observed learning curve with the exponent giving the best extrapolation.

conditions.value: JFT-300M examples seen; fit through 500M examples

rows.measure: Scaling exponent selected by interpolation versus extrapolation error
rows.note: The authors state that the best-fitting and best-extrapolating exponents differ despite overlapping fitted curves.
rows.check: Vision model, not an LM. V7 is not modality-specific, so the link stands. Baseline/value are the interpolation-best vs extrapolation-best exponents.

rows.subject: Six image-classification architectures (aggregate over 72 tasks)
rows.size_stated: Six architectures; individual parameter counts are listed in Table 1
rows.stage_stated: pretraining on JFT-300M; few-shot downstream evaluation
rows.operation_detail: Compare four scaling estimators' extrapolation across image-classification learning curves.

conditions.value: 72 combinations of architecture, downstream dataset and few-shot metric

rows.measure: Fraction of tasks in which each estimator achieves the best extrapolation error
rows.baseline: M1, M2 and M3 comparison methods
rows.value: M4 outperforms the other methods in more than 70% of tasks in this domain.
rows.note: This is the paper's aggregate statement for the image domain; the tasks use downstream few-shot accuracy/error rather than pretraining loss.
rows.check: This is the study's own estimator beating others (>70% of tasks). It does not show a power law holding in vision, so it is relinked from V5 to V7 (estimator choice matters). Power-law evidence for vision is in Figure 3 text; see missing.

rows.subject: 262M-parameter decoder-only transformer
rows.operation_detail: Fit scaling estimators on token-count learning curves and evaluate extrapolated few-shot BIG-Bench performance.
rows.measure: Extrapolation RMSE for task performance
rows.baseline: M1 and M2 perform equally well and worse than M3 and M4, according to the authors' summary.
rows.value: M3 and M4 perform best in this domain; Table 3 gives task- and shot-specific RMSEs.
rows.uncertainty: Table 3 reports ± values by task and shot; no uncertainty for the aggregate statement.
rows.note: The authors selected the five tasks with highest learnability; the aggregate statement does not give a single numerical score.
rows.check: This is an estimator comparison on downstream few-shot scores of one 262M model over tokens. The curves are noisy, and M1/M2 (power-law forms) are consistently worse than M3/M4. No single aggregate value is given; Table 3 per-task values are not recorded.
